hero.subtitle: The challenge-response authentication framework for HTTP

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
HTTP provides a general framework for access control and authentication via an extensible set of challenge-response authentication schemes. This document defines the HTTP Authentication framework, including the 401 and 407 status codes and the Authorization and Proxy-Authorization header fields.

This RFC defines the framework, not individual authentication schemes. Specific schemes like Basic (RFC 7617), Digest (RFC 7616), and Bearer (RFC 6750) are defined separately and plug into this framework.

sections.title: Authentication Framework
sections.content:
HTTP authentication is based on a simple challenge-response model. The server challenges the client with a 401 (Unauthorized) response, and the client retries with credentials in the Authorization header.

Challenge
The server issues a challenge via the WWW-Authenticate header, specifying one or more authentication schemes it supports.
Credentials
The client sends credentials via the Authorization header. The format depends on the authentication scheme (Basic, Bearer, Digest, etc.).
Realm
The realm parameter defines a protection space. Different realms on the same server may require different credentials.

sections.title: 401 and 407 Responses
sections.content:
Two status codes drive the authentication mechanism, one for origin servers and one for proxies.

Status
Challenge Header
Credentials Header
401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate
Authorization
407 Proxy Auth Required
Proxy-Authenticate
Proxy-Authorization

A 401 response MUST include a WWW-Authenticate header containing at least one challenge. Without this header, the client cannot determine which authentication scheme to use.

sections.title: Authorization Header
sections.content:
The Authorization header field allows a client to authenticate itself with an origin server. Its value consists of the authentication scheme followed by scheme-specific credentials.

Authorization Header Examples
Basic authentication (base64 encoded user:password):
Authorization: Basic dXNlcjpwYXNzd29yZA==

Bearer token (OAuth 2.0):
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...

Digest authentication:
Authorization: Digest username="user",
realm="example.com",
nonce="dcd98b...",
response="6629fae..."

Basic authentication transmits credentials in base64, which is trivially decoded. It MUST only be used over HTTPS. Bearer tokens provide better security but must also be protected in transit.

sections.title: WWW-Authenticate Header
sections.content:
The WWW-Authenticate header field indicates the authentication scheme(s) and parameters applicable to the target resource. A server MAY include multiple challenges.

WWW-Authenticate Examples
Single scheme:
WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="Simple API"

Multiple schemes:
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="api",
error="invalid_token"
WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="api"

Negotiate (SPNEGO/Kerberos):
WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate
Scheme Selection
When multiple schemes are offered, the client should choose the most secure scheme it supports. Browsers typically prefer Negotiate over Digest over Basic.
Protection Spaces
The realm parameter defines a protection space on the server. The client can reuse credentials for the same realm without waiting for another challenge.
